title: TA9-00239
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXX, the claimant, alleges he is a citizen of the People's Republic of China (PRC). He claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant alleges that he was first introduced to Christianity by a friend in XXXXXX 2007. The friend suggested Christianity to the claimant because he recognized that the claimant was feeling depressed due to his failed relationships. The claimant began to regularly attend underground services beginning in late XXXXXX 2007. In XXXX 2008, the claimant was at his underground house church service when it was raided by members of the Public Security Bureau (PSB). The claimant managed to escape and immediately went into hiding. The claimant alleges that PSB attended his home in search of him. The PSB told his parents that they had arrested four fellow members of the church and demanded that the claimant turn himself in. Fearing that he would be arrested, the claimant used the services of a smuggler to leave China for Canada where he filed for refugee protection.
The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The reasons are as follows.

The determinative issue in this claim is the identity of the claimant as a Christian and his risk of persecution by authorities in China. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's documentary and oral testimony in this regard is not credible. The reasons for this finding are noted below. Personal Identity
The claimant was able to establish his identity as a national of China with documents he submitted in support of his claim2 including his 2006 resident identity card and Hukou. Christian Identity

The claimant alleges that his religious profile is that of a devout Christian believer. The claimant alleges that he underwent a religious conversion in China after his friend spread the gospel to him. He alleged that he risked his personal safety in order to regularly attended underground Christian services in China. He alleges he read the bible and prayed daily. He alleges that because of his faith in God his life had new meaning. Since being in Canada, the claimant continues to pray and read the bible daily and attends church services 2 to 3 times per week.

The claimant was questioned with regard to his Christian knowledge and understanding. The claimant demonstrated some knowledge of Christianity; however, it does not necessarily mean he is genuine practicing Christian. While the claimant was able to provide answers to most fundamental questions, it was clear he did not have a clear understanding of the concept of the absolution of sin as it relates to the crucifixion and death of Jesus. The claimant testified that the death of Jesus absolved mankind of both original and personal sin. Christians believe that the absolution of original sin only comes through baptism. Counsel for the claimant argued the claimant is not a religious theologian and should not be held to a high standard with regard to his Christian knowledge. She further argued that there are many genuine Christians who may not know the distinction between the absolution of original sin and sins and general. The panel is not persuaded by counsel's argument. While it is true that there are many individuals who consider themselves to be genuine Christians who may not have well a developed knowledge of Christian beliefs, the panel must consider whether it is reasonable for the claimant not to be aware of this distinction. The claimant alleges he has been attending church services and bible study 2 to 3 times per week since November 2008 and that he has been reading the bible daily since September 2007. The claimant alleges that while in China he risked his personal safety to express his faith. It is reasonable to expect that a person with the religious profile of the claimant would have a deeper and more substantial understanding of the core beliefs of Christianity. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

The claimant was asked to provide a brief overview of what was contained in the gospel of Mathew. The claimant responded with some very broad statements but when asked to be more specific, he stated he was unable to recall. The claimant has alleged that he has been reading the bible daily for approximately 30 minutes a day since XXXXXX 2007. He also alleges that he has been attending church services and bible study classes 2 to 3 times per week since XXXXXX 2008. Given the claimant's alleges religious profile, it is reasonable to expect that he would have a better understanding of the gospels. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

Despite his stated testimonial failings, the claimant did demonstrate some Christian knowledge. The claimant produced a letter from Rev. XX together with a baptismal certificate and photographs3. These documents can only attest to the claimant's participation in church activities; they do not attest to his motivation.

In this regard, recent case law indicates that a pastor's assessment of the genuineness of a person's faith cannot be substituted for the assessment that the panel is required to make.4 The panel gives little evidentiary weight to the claimant's religious documents in assessing the claimant's religious genuineness. Arrest of Fellow Church Members and Pursuit of Claimant by the PSB

The claimant alleges that four of his fellow church members were arrested and incarcerated. The claimant was asked when he last heard that his fellow church members were incarcerated. The claimant's testimony in this regard was confusing and internally inconsistent. He was asked several times to clarify when he last heard that his fellow church members were still in custody. The claimant first testified that he last heard that they were still incarcerated from his parents when they talked with the relatives of his fellow church members. In this response, the claimant mentioned "six months" but he was not clear if he meant that they had spoken with them six months following the raid or six months ago. When asked to clarify what he meant when he stated "six months" the claimant responded that his parents has actually spoken with the relatives of his fellow church members in XXXX 2011 and that was when he learned that they were still in custody. The claimant was given several opportunities to explain the inconsistency with his previous testimony however, the claimant was unable to provide a reasonable explanation. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's internally inconsistent testimony concerning the continuing incarceration of his fellow church members.

The claimant's testimony in this regard to the arrest of his fellow church members runs counter to the country condition documents, which will be demonstrated later in these reasons with the analysis of the Situation of Christians in Guangdong Province. In addition, the claimant has provided no persuasive documentary evidence to support his allegation that he is being pursued by the PSB. The sole basis for his claim that he is being pursed by the PSB is his testimony and the allegations he has made in his Personal Information Form (PIF).5

The claimant alleges that the PSB have attended his home on 14 occasions with the intent of arresting him, however, he acknowledges that the PSB did not leave or show his parents a summons or a warrant. Country condition documents6 indicate that a summons is generally left with or shown to family members when the police want someone to come to their headquarters. In addition, the summons is the documentary basis for the subsequent issuance of an arrest warrant if the person in whom they are interested does not respond to the summons. Although this policy is not always implemented, it is reasonable that one would have been issued in respect of the claimant, given that the claimant testified that the PSB have attended his home in search of him on 14 occasions. The claimant also alleged that the PSB have continued their pursuit of him and as recently as XXX 2011. The alleged actions of the PSB would indicate that they had more than a casual interest in the claimant. Given the relentless and persistent pursuit of the claimant by the PSB, it is reasonable to expect that if the PSB and already arrested 4 of the 12 members of his church and were intent on arresting the claimant that they would have taken the effort to issue a summons or a warrant for him. The lack of a summons when one should reasonably have been issued damages the credibility of the claimant.

On the basis of the subsequent analysis on the Situation of Christians in Guangdong Province and in the context of the findings and negative inferences drawn above, and the lack of persuasive evidence to the contrary, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's allegation that there was a raid on his house church and that four of his fellow church members were arrested and incarcerated, is neither plausible nor credible.

Having found that the claimant's church was not raided and that he is not being pursued by the PSB, and, in the context of his Christian knowledge, the panel finds that the claimant was not a Christian in China as he alleges. The panel further finds that the claimant's allegation that he was a practicing Christian in China is not credible and was made only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent claim.

While it is difficult to make a judgment regarding the genuineness of a persons' religious practice it is necessary in this case. In doing so, the panel considered the totality of the evidence available. With respect to the claimant's religious affiliation, the panel must consider whether the claimant is a genuine practicing Christian in this country. There is a requirement for 'good faith' in making a refugee claim. In this regard, R.P.G. Haines, the Chairman of a refugee status appeal panel and A.G. Wang Heed, a member of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees stated in part: If there is no good faith requirement in the sur place situation, it places in the hands of the appellant for refugee status the means of unilaterally determining the grant to him or her of refugee status.7

In this regard, the panel cites the following from James Hathaway's The Law of Refugee Status with regard to "sur place" claims: An individual who as a stratagem deliberately manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution, which did not exist, cannot be said to belong to this category.8

Having previously found the claimant's testimony with regard to his religious affiliation in China untrustworthy, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of all of the findings and negative inferences drawn above, that his claim has not been made in good faith.

Having found that his claim has not been made in good faith, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of the findings noted above, that the claimant joined a Christian church in Canada only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim. In the context, as noted above, and on the basis of the totality of evidence disclosed and in the context of the claimant's knowledge of Christianity, the panel finds that the claimant is not a genuine practicing Christian, nor would he be perceived to be in China. Situation of Christians in Guangdong Province

Notwithstanding the foregoing determination, the panel recognizes that refugee laws are forward looking. In this regard, the panel has considered whether there is a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if he chooses to continue to practice Christianity in an unregistered church in China. The claimant is from Guangdong province and alleges that he has lived there most of his life. The panel notes that the documentary evidence states as follows: ...the Executive Secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council commented that Fujian and Guangdong have "the most liberal policy on religion in China, especially on Christianity" (Executive Secretary 1 Sept. 2005a). In his travels, the Executive Secretary has met with local authorities who, he said, usually tolerate activities of unregistered Christian groups (ibid.). While authorities are of a more tolerant nature in rural areas than in urban centres, they would usually take steps to discourage religious activity if it had a link to groups from outside China (ibid.). The Executive Secretary stated that he is aware of a number of unregistered churches that have been allowed to function for years (ibid.). Though he has received a few reports of arrests of Catholic priests in the years 2003 to 2005, the Executive Secretary noted that overall, Christians in Fujian and Guangdong "enjoy one of the most liberal polic[ies] on religious freedom in China." (ibid.).

The Executive Secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council recently stated in June 14, 2010 correspondence, that the Chinese authorities have demonstrated a high degree of tolerance to Christian activities in general and particularly towards non-registered groups.

The panel also notes that though there were arrests and incidents of persecution of Christians documented in 2005, 2006, 2007 2008, and 2009, none of these arrests or incidents of persecution were noted as being in Guangdong province. In 2005, there were reports of house church crackdowns in the provinces of Shanxi, Henan, Hubei, Jiangxi, and Jilin and in May 2005, Chinese officials coordinated raids on 100 house churches in Jilin province [northeast China], arresting approximately 600 Christians. During the year, there were also reports of similar incidents in Hebei, Xinjiang, Beijing and Shanghai. The U.S. 2009 International Religious Freedom Report specifically reviews arrests and incidents of persecution of Christians in China in 2008, 2009 and in early 2010 notes arrests of Christians in Beijing, Shanghai, the XUAR, Jilin province, Hebei province, Henan province, Zhegiang province, Anhui province, Hubei province, Sichuan province, Heilongjiang province, Inner Mongolia, and Shandong province. No mention is made of arrests or incidents of persecution of Christians in Guangdong province. I have reviewed the most recent items in the exhibits covering 2008 and 2009 and 2010 and have noted arrests and incidents of persecution of Christians in Beijing, Shanghai, Shanxi province, Jilin province, Xinjiang province, Guizhou province, Hubei province, Hebei province, Inner Mongolia, the XUAR, Henan province, Sichuan province, Shandong province, Zhejiang province, Anhui province, Jiangsu province, and Heilongjiang province, but none in Guangdong province. The panel has reviewed all of the documentary evidence submitted and has found no persuasive, recent evidence of arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Christians in Guangdong province.

The Annual Report of Persecution by the Government on Christian Churches within Mainland China very specifically notes the arrests and incidents of persecution of Christians in China from January 2009 to December 2009, but no arrests or incidents of persecution occurred in Guangdong province where the claimant is from. This report states that during 2008, the number of Christians persecuted in all of China was 2,935 and that the number of Christians arrested and detained was 389. The panel has reviewed all the documentary evidence submitted and finds no persuasive evidence of recent arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Christians in Guangdong province. The claimant's underground house church is located in Guangdong Province and was comprised of only 12 members. While underground churches are usually tolerated in Guangdong province, it is noted that in December 2008 the Liangren Church in Guangzhou City was raided. This incident was noted in the Annual Report of Persecution by the Government on Christian Churches within Mainland China, published by the United States based China Aid Association, which specifically notes arrests as well as evidence of persecution in various provinces. The Liangren church had more than sixty members. In addition, the pastor of that church was permitted to submit an application for administrative reconsideration. While it is not known what the results of the administrative reconsideration were, it must be noted that there were no arrests and no one was sentenced as a result of the raid. Further information contained in China Aid Association report identifies that a church with 200 members was moved to another district. As well, the same report indicates that 3 churches were expelled and 3 Christian schools aborted, however it is not clear why the churches were expelled or why the schools were aborted. It is unclear what the circumstances were that led to the aborting of the schools or what type churches were expelled or the reason they were expelled. In fact, it is unclear what is meant by the term expelled in this context. As such, the panel can give little weight to these documents in determining incidents of persecution. What is clear, however, is that no one was arrested in any of these incidents and no one was reported abused. Although country document information regarding China generally provides mixed messages concerning the suppression of underground church activity, the lack of any information regarding any instance of arrest for Guangdong Province, is significant and convincing.

Counsel for the claimant submitted country condition documents9 in support of the claimant's allegations. Counsel referred to pages 203 to 208 of her country condition package10 which cites a 2010 China Aid Association document in which it is identified that the pastor of the Liangren Church continues to be harassed by authorities and has been arrested and interrogated several times over the past two years. This report suggests that the pastor was accused of "sedition" for having posted articles on the Internet. The report also suggests that the pastor is being harassed because of his intention to hold large outdoor services. These documents suggest that there is heightened interest with this pastor because of his desire to hold large services in pubic places. In this regard, the incidents associated to the Liangren church are distinguished from other underground churches that conduct their services in private settings. In any event, the PSB have only shown interest in the Pastor and there is no indications that any lay persons were arrested or have ever been arrested in connection with Liangren church.

The panel has considered all of the documents submitted about the situation for Christians in China, specifically the articles and reports documenting arrests and persecution and finds, on a balance of probabilities, that if there were recent arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Christians in Guangdong province, there would be some documentation of these arrests or incidents of persecution by reliable sources.

The panel has considered that the China Aid Association (CAA), and its president, Bob Fu, have stated in its report that they have not documented all cases of persecution and religious repression, which has occurred in every province in China, including Guangdong and Fujian. However, I note again that there has been no persuasive evidence of recent arrests or incidents of persecution of lay Christians in Guangdong province in any of the documentation regarding religious persecution in China.

According to the U.S. Department of State International Freedom of Religion Report, the extent of religious freedom in China continues to vary widely within the country. That report notes that unregistered religious groups have continued to expand and that most Christian groups, the majority of which are not registered, no longer operate in strict secrecy and in fact carried out public activities including convening seminars, publishing materials, renting space for offices and events, and disseminating information on the Internet. Many unregistered religious groups also carried out social service work. In parts of the country, unregistered groups grew rapidly and authorities did not pressure them to register. In some areas, officials did little to interfere with the worship or social service activities of unregistered churches. It is noted that at least 20 million Chinese citizens worship in official churches and that 50 to 70 million worship in unregistered churches. Some unregistered church groups were able to hold meetings that hundreds attended without interference. Some unregistered groups had significant membership, properties, financial resources and networks. The government has granted approval for an increasing number of religious books to be published and the number of Christian websites on the Internet increased. The panel finds that the situation in Guangdong province does not reflect what is happening in many other provinces where there have been arrests and incidents of persecution of ordinary Christians.

The British Home Office Report notes that there are fifty to seventy million Protestant Christians in China who practice without state sanction and that only twenty million practice their religion in state approved churches. That report also states that prayer meetings and Bible study groups held among friends and families need not register with authorities. The article, "Church and State in China" by K. K. Yeo, states that only gatherings of believers with more than 40 people are required by law to register with the government. Again, the claimant alleges that her church was comprised of only 32 members and during their gatherings, they would recite and discuss Bible passages and pray.

The panel recognizes that even if the evidence speaks of some harm that would qualify as serious, the Refugee Protection Division must consider whether there is a serious possibility that the harm will actually come to pass. A statute, which outlaws the claimant's conduct or characteristic, may be in existence, and it may provide for unconscionably severe punishment for that conduct or characteristic, but this does not necessarily mean there is a serious possibility that the punishment will be inflicted on the claimant. The Supreme Court has emphasized that, in a determination as to whether the claimant's fear is objectively well founded, the relevant factors include the laws in the claimant's homeland, together with the manner in which they are applied. In this connection, the Court cited paragraph 43 of the UNHCR Handbook. Enforcement measures may vary from area to area within a country, and if this is the case, "the reasonableness of a fear of persecution depends, inter alia, on the practices of the relevant local authority". A pattern of non-enforcement might imply that there is less than a serious possibility.11

As has been discussed, the supporting documentary evidence for the claimant's home province of Guangdong indicates, the risk of persecution for practicing Christians is low. The panel has considered the documentary evidence about conditions in Guangdong province and the claimant's personal circumstances. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant would be able to practice his religion, worshiping in the Christian congregation of his choosing, if he were to return to his home in Guangdong province in China and that there is not a serious possibility that he would be persecuted for doing so.

The panel has chosen to rely on the documentary evidence because it originates from a variety of reputable independent sources, which would reasonably be expected to be knowledgeable with respect to the situation of Christians in Guangdong. The documentary evidence is seen as reliable, probative, detailed information, so as to provide the panel with a thorough understanding of the situation of the Christian Church in Guangdong province.

The panel is supported in this decision by a recent decision by Mr. Justice Russell. This decision concerns an alleged raid in Guangdong Province. In reaching his decision, Mr. Justice Russell cited Justice Crampton's decision in Nen Mei Lin12 concerning Fujian province in which the court stated that in the context of the significant detail in the documentation regarding the dates and locations of arrests and other steps taken to discourage Christian activity in China, it was reasonable for the Board to conclude that if persecution of members of underground churches occurred in Fujian province it would have been documented. In addition, Justice Lemieux in Jiang noted that the documentary evidence concerning Fujian province indicates there is a minimum of constraints on religious practice and people generally practice their religion freely.

Further, in Yu,13 Justice Zinn noted that the only evidence provided to the Board regarding the alleged raid was the claimant's own testimony. It was further noted that although the claimant in that case had been found to be credible in regard to his Christian identity and membership in a house church, there was documentary evidence before the Board that brought his evidence of the raid into question and led to an inference that no such raid occurred.

On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the cumulative findings and negative inferences noted above, the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim. (signed) "L. Favreau" L.
